title: The Visualiser: The Complete Guide
author: Jamie Clark
summary: Jamie Clark delivers a comprehensive, evidence-grounded guide to the visualiser -- the document camera or tablet-mirroring setup that projects teacher and student work in real time -- arguing it is one of the most powerful instructional tools available precisely because it makes thinking visible rather than just products. The article grounds the case for visualisers in three research traditions: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction (present material in small steps, provide worked examples), Cognitive Load Theory (reduce extraneous load by making layout perceptually available), and Dual Coding Theory (simultaneously verbal and visual channels produce more durable learning). Clark maps five practical uses across an explicit lesson structure -- live modelling, mid-task feedback, whole-class feedback the following lesson, live diagramming, and peer work display -- with concrete scripted examples for each. A key pedagogical insight is that the most powerful use is showing the construction of a model in real time, including hesitations and corrections, rather than displaying a finished product; the impermanence of the mini-whiteboard under the visualiser is the point, because students see that thinking is revisable, not fixed. The guide notes that a physical camera is not required -- an iPad or Surface tablet mirrored to a classroom screen achieves the same effect.
points: * The visualiser's distinctive advantage over a whiteboard is that the teacher faces the class throughout -- eye contact and monitoring never stop -- while still writing or modelling in real time, eliminating the instructional dead zone of turning one's back to the room. * Showing the construction of a response live, including hesitations, corrections, and wipe-and-redo moments, is more instructionally powerful than displaying a finished model because it externalises expert thinking and makes the decision-making process, not just the output, visible to students. * Cognitive Load Theory predicts the visualiser's effect: when layout and process are perceptually available rather than imagined, students can direct working memory to the actual intellectual work of the lesson rather than to logistics. * Doug Lemov's Show Call -- placing a student's work under the visualiser mid-task without prior warning -- changes the quality of independent practice because students know any piece of work might be projected; the accountability effect operates through anticipation, not just consequence. * Whole-class feedback delivered the next lesson via visualiser -- projecting a strong response and a common-error response, annotating both live while students revise their own work in a different colour -- is more actionable than written comments because it is shared, immediate, and modelled.
quotes: A visualiser is a mounted document camera that projects whatever sits beneath it onto a screen or whiteboard in real time. Unlike modelling at a whiteboard, it allows the teacher to face the class throughout. Eye contact and monitoring never stop and the classroom stays in view.

The most powerful use is showing the work in progress, not the polished product. A mini-whiteboard placed under the visualiser is the ideal modelling surface. It's erasable, so the teacher can revise, cross out, and redo in real time. The impermanence is the point because students see that thinking is revisable, not fixed.

Barak Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction are closely aligned with the practice of visualising work live in the classroom. The principles emphasise presenting new material in small steps, providing worked examples, and demonstrating what success looks like before students attempt independent practice.

John Sweller's research established that working memory is limited and easily overwhelmed. When students have to simultaneously decode verbal instructions, imagine a visual layout, and recall content knowledge, cognitive load can become unmanageable. The visualiser reduces that load by making one element -- the layout and process -- perceptually available rather than imagined.

When a teacher narrates aloud while modelling under a visualiser -- 'I'm going to write my topic sentence here, and I'm going to keep it to one sentence, not two, because...' -- students receive information simultaneously through verbal and visual channels. Research on dual coding by Allan Paivio and later work by Richard E. Mayer suggests that learning becomes more durable when words and visuals are meaningfully combined.

Place a strong response under the visualiser (with the student's permission, or anonymised). Talk through what makes it effective. Then place a response with a common error and model the correction live. Students annotate their own work as you go.

Doug Lemov calls a version of this Show Call -- picking up a student's work mid-task and projecting it without warning. The accountability effect is significant: when students know any piece of work might go under the camera, the quality of independent practice changes.
